3. **Granary weight.** Where the county's tax rice waits, a knob (research/questions/0098-storehouses-for-the-tax-rice.drawing.html): a county on navigable water leans to a row of storehouses at the town's river landing, its rice moving through, and its office keeps one modest storehouse; an isolated county leans to the office's own storehouse, which keeps the rice. The office draws ONE storehouse either way - the landing row is off the compound's sheet. Read the county's Mode B geography to pick. An upland county's granary also shifts CONTENTS: more in-kind goods (soybeans, barley, local products), since less of its tax is rice (see grounding).

For night-soil specifically: in L7R, burakumin handle this for samurai and wealthy merchants (matching L5R canon); farmers and other tenant peasants handle their own, because they need the fertilizer and could not plausibly afford to outsource. (L5R-era materials called this caste "eta" - L7R has dropped that term as a real-world slur and uses "burakumin" throughout; [`setting/castes.md`](https://github.com/EliAndrewC/gm-assistant/blob/main/setting/castes.md).)

- **A tub stands OUTSIDE the building and CLEAR of it - no part of the glyph may lie in the footprint** (GM rule 2026-07-25, tightened from "center outside" to "no overlap at all" 2026-07-26; checked by `make pack-audit` `tubs_in_buildings`, reported as TUB IN BUILDING). The two reasons are the two things the tub is for: a *tensuioke* is filled by the **downspout**, which discharges at the outside wall, and it is emptied by a **bucket line**, which forms in the open where people can reach it. A tub drawn into the footprint is fed by nothing and stands where nobody can get at it - and if the building is already burning, a water butt inside it is exactly where the water is not. So the tub's own glyph sits just clear of the outside wall face (2.2 px, ~0.7 ft at 3 px = 1 ft - the house style on all three pool manors, so its outline clears the wall's ink): far enough out to be under the eaves-line and in the open, close enough that a downspout reaches it.
